title: Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 1–2)
hookLine: a woman prays so hard the priest thinks she's drunk, then sings like Mary will

lines: NO CHILDREN, AND A RIVAL'S TAUNTS.
AN OLD PRIEST ON A STOOL, WATCHING.
cards: Every year a family travels up to the sanctuary at Shiloh, and every year it's the worst week for one of them. Her name is Hannah, Anna in the Douay-Rheims.

Her husband loves her, but she has no children, and his other wife has many and needles her about it, year after year, until Hannah can't eat. Her husband tries to help: Am I not better to thee than ten children?
It doesn't help. So one year, after the meal, she goes to the doorway of the house of the Lord and starts to pray. An old priest named Eli is sitting there on a stool, watching.

teach.b: Hannah prays with tears. Her lips move, but no sound comes out. People usually prayed aloud then, so to Eli she looks drunk.
He tells her to go sleep it off.

teach.h: I HAVE POURED OUT MY SOUL.
teach.b: She answers him, in the Douay: "I am an exceeding unhappy woman, and have drunk neither wine nor any strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the Lord." Not a polite request: everything in her, poured out.
And Eli, to his credit, changes his tune: go in peace, and may God grant your petition.

teach.h: HER FACE WAS NO MORE SAD.
teach.b: After that, the text says, her face was no longer sad. Nothing has happened yet. She simply prayed and was heard.
Then she has a son, Samuel, and when he's weaned she brings him back to Shiloh and gives him to the Lord's service, just as she vowed. And she sings: "My heart hath rejoiced in the Lord."

teach.h: A SONG THAT MARY WILL ECHO.
teach.b: Her song turns the world upside down: the mighty are broken, the weak are girded with strength, the hungry are filled, and God lifts the poor from the dust to sit with princes.

teach.h: MY HEART HATH REJOICED IN THE LORD.
teach.b: Centuries later, a young woman named Mary visits her cousin and sings: my soul doth magnify the Lord, he hath put down the mighty and exalted the humble, filled the hungry with good things.
The Church has long heard Hannah's song as the older sister of Mary's Magnificat, and prays it among the Old Testament canticles in the Liturgy of the Hours.

how: Catholics pray Hannah's song as one of the Old Testament canticles in the Liturgy of the Hours, at Morning Prayer, and many couples hoping for a child find company in her story.

o: a set prayer the priests recited at Shiloh
the blessing Eli spoke over Hannah's son
a silent, tearful prayer that later became a song

p: the son she gave to the Lord

s: Hannah prayed loudly, which is why Eli noticed her
her lips moved, but her voice was not heard. that's why he thought she was drunk.
after praying, her face was no longer sad, before anything had changed
she went her way and ate, and her countenance was no more changed.
Hannah's song and Mary's Magnificat share images
both sing of God bringing down the mighty and filling the hungry.

games.q: you're Hannah. you've prayed your heart out in silence, and the priest accuses you of being drunk. what do you do?
o: leave in shame without a word.
tell him the truth: you've poured out your soul before the Lord.
argue with him and storm off.
games.why: she answers him honestly, and Eli blesses her: go in peace. a priest learns to read a broken heart, and she leaves no longer sad.

practice: Think of what you've carried the longest, the ache you don't bring up anymore because people are tired of hearing it, or you are, and don't tidy it.
If you pray, tell God exactly how it is, silently, the way Hannah did, with no polite words in front; if not, say it plainly to yourself. Then stay a moment, and notice your face.

wordCard.voice: Hannah's prayer. A silent, tearful prayer at Shiloh, so intense the priest thought she was drunk, and later a song of joy that Mary's Magnificat echoes. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Hannah, a name related to the word for grace or favor. The Latin and the Douay call her Anna.

carryVoice: Your line: she poured out her soul. Eli saw a drunk; God heard a prayer. Day three hundred ninety-seven, in the books.
